finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches an attacker-supplied URL server-side. The only check is that the value is a string starting with https://, which does not restrict host, IP range, port, or redirect targets. Attacker can reach internal TLS services directly or use an https:// URL that 302-redirects to internal http:// endpoints such as 169.254.169.254. Impact is blind: only the response byte length is returned.
finding.source: server.js:10 req.body.avatarUrl (unauthenticated POST body, parsed at server.js:5)
finding.sink: server.js:14 axios.get(url, { responseType: "arraybuffer" }) with default redirect following

trace.note: Validation: typeof string and startsWith('https://') only; no host, IP, port, or redirect checks
Server issues request to url; axios follows redirects by default, so the https:// check is not applied to redirect targets; no timeout or size limit
Only img.data.length is returned, so the response body is not exposed (blind SSRF)

finding.guards_checked: Type check (server.js:11) and https:// scheme prefix (server.js:11) only. No host allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local IP block, no DNS resolution check, no port restriction, no redirect validation, no timeout or size cap. Userinfo-style host tricks (https://x@169.254.169.254/) pass the prefix check but are unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is server.js:11, a typeof string test plus a startsWith("https://") prefix test. That is a prefix check, not a closing guard. No host, IP, port, or redirect validation exists anywhere in server.js, and there is no auth middleware on the route (server.js:5 is express.json() only).
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: req.body.avatarUrl (server.js:10) is passed unchecked beyond a https:// prefix (server.js:11) into axios.get with default redirect following (server.js:14), and only img.data.length is returned (server.js:15). The route is unauthenticated, so an attacker controls the request target and can use https:// URLs that redirect to internal hosts.

finding.claim: Candidate ruled out, not SSRF: GET /users/:id uses a constant host (USER_SVC) and encodeURIComponent (server.js:19) blocks escape from the /v1/users/ path. Bare '.' or '..' segments can normalize to same-host paths such as /v1/, which is path traversal within the users service, not SSRF.
finding.guards_checked: encodeURIComponent (server.js:19); constant base URL (server.js:7). Host cannot be changed by the attacker.

verdict.guard_found: encodeURIComponent at server.js:19 stops "/", "?", "#" from altering the path, and the base URL is the constant USER_SVC defined at server.js:7 and used at server.js:20, so the attacker cannot change the host.
verdict.reason: The sink at server.js:20 always goes to the fixed host in USER_SVC (server.js:7), and the attacker-controlled id is only a path segment after encodeURIComponent (server.js:19), so this is not SSRF; at most a path manipulation within the users service, as the candidate itself notes.
